headline: Skip the Slop — the Real Bite's Inside Jones Inlet After Dark
subhead: While the fleet fights a beat-up ocean front for bluefish, the jetty rocks and channel edges are quietly producing bass, fluke, and a weakfish comeback nobody's talking about.
body_markdown:
Everybody and their brother is parked on the ocean beach at first light this week, watching bunker schools get bulldozed by blues in three feet of whitewater, getting their teeth rattled by a 3.9-foot swell that never lays down long enough to fish it right. I get it — a bluefish blitz is a hell of a thing to watch. But I've been running the other way. Dead low tide, I'm walking out on the west jetty at Jones Inlet with a bag of eels and a bucket of bunker chunks, and I'm not fighting anybody for water.

Here's the thing about that ocean front right now — 71-degree water stacked up against a short, choppy period like that isn't fishable water, it's washing-machine water. The bass know it. They've gone almost completely nocturnal on us, same as they have from here down through Jersey, and that's not new — we flagged that pattern last week and it's held right through the heat. During the day these fish are sitting deep on structure, tucked into current seams off the rocks or holding on the edge of the channel where the water's a couple degrees cooler than the flats around it. You want them, you come back after the sun drops.

My program right now is simple. I fish the last two hours of the outgoing into the start of the incoming, right at the Jones Inlet jetty where the current rips past the rocks. Whole bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, 4/0 circle hook, just enough weight to hold bottom in that current — 3 to 4 ounces depending on how hard it's ripping. Eels are the other play, snap-swum slow along the rock face on the drift. I put two overslot bass in the box Tuesday night working that exact stretch between 10 and midnight, both fish sitting right where the current breaks off the last rock pile before it dumps into the main channel. Not a rod-bending blitz — one bite an hour if you're lucky — but real fish, 32 and 34 inches, and nobody else on the jetty to share the spot with.

Now the bluefish — that pattern's still the most dependable thing going in this zone, and we called that too. Bunker are thick, and every time the tide pushes them through the inlet mouth or pins them against the beach off Short Beach and the west end of Jones, the blues show up and tear into them. Poppers and Hopkins Shorty 3-ounces off the beach when you can find a lull in the swell, or bunker chunks fished from a boat working the edge of the bait school inside the inlet where it's calmer. This bite is still building and I'd expect it to keep spreading — more bait pushing through means more windows, even with the ocean beat up the way it is.

Fluke's a mixed bag right now, and I'll be straight with you — the shallow bay flats have gone quiet. Too warm, too still. What's still producing is exactly what you'd expect: the deeper channel bends and the inlet-adjacent water where there's current moving and the bottom stays cooler. Sloop Channel is still your best bet, drifting the deeper bends on the outgoing with 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet in white or pink shine, working it right along the channel edge where it drops from six feet to fifteen. I had three keeper fluke to 21 inches out there Sunday morning on the last of the ebb, mixed in with a pile of shorts that tells me there's a lot of fish around, just not all of them measuring up yet.

And here's the one that's got guys at the dock talking — weakfish are actually showing back up in the bay. Not in numbers like the old days, but I've had reports of legal fish coming out of the deeper holes off Freeport and up toward the Wantagh Bridge, mostly on the evening bite as the light drops and the water settles. Small bucktails, quarter-ounce, worked slow along bottom, or a bare hook with a piece of squid if the current's soft. It's not a fishery yet, it's a rumor with fish attached to it — but a rumor worth checking on a quiet tide.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full in early August and that means more current, which is exactly what this whole pattern needs to sharpen up. If the ocean stays beat up — and with that period and wave height I don't expect it to clean up fast — I'd keep my time inside the inlet and in the channels where moving water does the work for you. If I had one night this week to fish, I'd take the jetty at the top of the outgoing, eel in hand, and let the current seam do the talking. Just don't expect company out there. That's kind of the point.
